questions.question: What is the purpose of 'Practice Set A — Basic'?
options: To test only the most advanced techniques
To reinforce fundamental, single-technique coding rules before moving to more complex combinations
To skip straight to mixed coding
To only test word length coding
questions.rationale: Practice Set A focuses on reinforcing fundamental, single-technique coding rules, building a solid base before more complex combinations are introduced.

questions.question: What does 'Practice Set B — Intermediate' likely introduce, compared to Set A?
options: Only easier variations of Set A
Combinations of two techniques, or slightly less common rule types, building on the basics
No new material at all
Only word length coding
questions.rationale: Set B builds on the basics by introducing combinations of two techniques or slightly less common rule types, a step up in complexity from Set A.

questions.question: What does 'Practice Set C — Advanced' likely require?
options: Only the simplest single-step rules
Correctly identifying and applying more complex or multi-step coding rules under less obvious conditions
No verification at all
Ignoring all previously learned rules
questions.rationale: Set C requires correctly identifying and applying more complex, multi-step rules, often under less obvious or more challenging conditions.

questions.question: What does 'Practice Set D — Challenge' likely test?
options: Only basic single-technique rules
The ability to flexibly apply the full range of techniques to unusual or tricky problems, not just standard cases
Nothing beyond Set A
Only word length coding
questions.rationale: The Challenge tier tests flexible application of the full range of techniques to unusual or tricky problems, beyond just standard, expected cases.

questions.question: Why does this lesson use four progressively harder practice tiers rather than one mixed set?
options: The ordering is arbitrary and has no purpose
To let learners build confidence and skill systematically before tackling the hardest, most ambiguous problems
Because harder problems don't build on easier ones
Because mixing difficulty levels is always more effective
questions.rationale: Progressive tiers let learners build confidence and skill systematically, ensuring a solid foundation before tackling the hardest, most ambiguous problems.

questions.question: What foundational skill from earlier parts does EVERY practice tier ultimately rely on?
options: Guessing without verification
Correctly identifying the coding rule by comparing input and output systematically, and verifying it against all given data
Ignoring alphabet wrap-around
Only checking a single example
questions.rationale: Every tier, regardless of difficulty, ultimately relies on the same foundational skill: systematically identifying the rule and verifying it fully against all given data.

questions.question: Why is it recommended to complete Practice Set A before attempting Practice Set D?
options: The sets are entirely unrelated
Because later, harder problems build on and combine the simpler techniques introduced and reinforced in the earlier sets
Because Set D never actually uses techniques from Set A
Because Set A is more difficult than Set D
questions.rationale: The harder practice sets build on and combine the simpler techniques first introduced and reinforced in the earlier sets, making the earlier practice a necessary foundation.

questions.question: What is one likely reason an 'Advanced' tier problem might use 'mixed coding' (combining two or more techniques)?
options: To make the problem impossible to solve
To test whether the learner can correctly identify and apply more than one rule together, not just recognize a single simple pattern
Because mixed coding is actually simpler than single-technique coding
Because Advanced problems never use single techniques
questions.rationale: Mixed coding at the Advanced tier tests whether a learner can correctly identify and combine multiple rules together, a more demanding skill than recognizing one simple pattern alone.

questions.question: In a Basic-tier problem using a simple +1 shift, what would DOG become?
options: CNF
EPH
DPG
COG
questions.rationale: Shifting each letter of DOG forward by 1: D->E, O->P, G->H, giving EPH.

questions.question: Why is timing yourself while working through these practice tiers a useful exam-preparation habit?
options: Timing has no relevance to solving accuracy
It helps build the speed needed to apply the high-speed detection techniques reliably under real time-pressured exam conditions
It replaces the need to actually verify rules
It only matters for the Basic tier
questions.rationale: Timed practice builds the speed and fluency needed to reliably apply the high-speed detection techniques under the real time pressure of an actual exam.
